title: The Masnavi (Masnavi-yi Ma‘navi)
author: Jalal al-Din Rumi

glance.label: Poet
glance.value: Jalal al-Din Muhammad Rumi (1207–1273), called Mawlana, 'our master' (Turkish Mevlana); born in the region of Balkh, in present-day Afghanistan and Tajikistan, and active for most of his life in Konya, in Anatolia

glance.label: Full title
glance.value: Masnavi-yi Ma‘navi, 'Rhyming Couplets of Inner Meaning', often translated 'The Spiritual Couplets'

glance.label: Composed
glance.value: Over the last fifteen years or so of Rumi's life, from about 1258–1262 until his death in December 1273; the prologue to Book II dates the resumption of work after a pause to 662 AH (1263–64)

glance.label: Dedicatee and scribe
glance.value: Husam al-Din Chalabi, Rumi's disciple and deputy, who asked for the poem, wrote it down from Rumi's dictation and read it back for correction

glance.label: Language and form
glance.value: Persian, in rhyming couplets (masnavi form) in the ramal metre; each Book has a short prose preface, and each after the first opens with an address to Husam al-Din

glance.label: Length
glance.value: Six Books, about 25,600 couplets in R. A. Nicholson's critical text; Book VI breaks off unfinished

glance.label: Method
glance.value: Stories nested inside stories, interrupted by commentary, prayer, Qur'anic and hadith quotation and passages of direct teaching

glance.label: Models
glance.value: The didactic masnavis of Sana'i (the Hadiqat al-haqiqa) and Farid al-Din 'Attar (the Ilahi-nama and Mantiq al-tayr)

glance.label: Afterlife
glance.value: Recited and expounded in the Mevlevi order founded around Rumi's tomb in Konya; a line often attributed to Jami calls it 'the Qur'an in the Persian tongue'

glance.label: Translations on this site
glance.value: E. H. Whinfield's abridged version of all six Books (1887; 2nd ed. 1898), and J. W. Redhouse's version of Book I (1881)

context: Jalal al-Din Muhammad was born in 1207 in the eastern Persian world, in or near Balkh (Franklin Lewis argues for the small town of Vakhsh, where his father then taught). His father, Baha al-Din Walad, was a preacher and jurist with mystical leanings. In the years before the Mongol invasions the family travelled west, by way of Mecca and Syria, and settled around 1229 in Konya, the capital of the Seljuk sultans of Rum, that is of the former Byzantine lands of Anatolia; the name 'Rumi', 'the man from Rum', comes from this. After his father's death in 1231 Jalal al-Din succeeded him as a teacher of religious law, was trained in the Sufi path by his father's disciple Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq, and studied in Aleppo and Damascus. By his mid-thirties he was a respected scholar and preacher with a circle of students [[lewis2000]] [[schimmel1978]].

In November 1244 a wandering dervish, Shams al-Din of Tabriz, arrived in Konya, and the encounter transformed Rumi's life. The two became inseparable; Rumi neglected his students, who resented the stranger, and Shams left for Syria. Rumi sent his son Sultan Walad to bring him back, but around 1247 Shams vanished for good. Later hagiographers say he was murdered with the connivance of Rumi's family, but the story cannot be proved, and Lewis treats it with caution. Shams's own recorded sayings, the Maqalat, show a sharp, demanding and learned teacher, not merely the 'wild' figure of legend. From this friendship came the outpouring of lyric poetry known as the Divan-i Shams-i Tabrizi, in which Rumi often signs his poems with his friend's name [[lewis2000]] [[chittick2004]] [[okane2002]].

The Masnavi belongs to the last part of Rumi's life. After Shams and then the goldsmith Salah al-Din Zarkub, the companion of his middle years (d. 1258), Rumi's closest disciple was Husam al-Din Chalabi. According to the hagiographer Aflaki, Husam asked Rumi for a book of teaching in the manner of Sana'i and 'Attar, and Rumi drew from his turban the eighteen opening couplets on the reed-flute. The rest of the poem was dictated, often in sessions of music and recitation, written down by Husam and read back to the poet. A pause followed Book I, which Aflaki connects with the death of Husam's wife; the prologue to Book II gives the date of the resumption as 662 AH (1263–64). Rumi died in Konya on 17 December 1273, with Book VI unfinished [[lewis2000]] [[okane2002]] [[nicholson1925]].

The poem's form is the masnavi, the Persian genre of long narrative or didactic poetry in rhyming couplets, and its models are the mystical masnavis of Sana'i of Ghazna and 'Attar of Nishapur, from whom Rumi borrows several stories. It is not organised as a treatise or a single narrative. Rumi tells animal fables (some from the Indian Kalila wa Dimna tradition), anecdotes of prophets, caliphs and saints, comic and sometimes obscene tales of townsmen and peasants, and parables from the Qur'an, and he breaks into them constantly to explain, digress and pray. The poem is saturated with the Qur'an and the sayings of the Prophet, and its Arabic preface to Book I presents it as the 'roots of the roots of the roots of religion' and the unveiling of the mysteries of union and certainty [[nicholson1925]] [[debruijn1997]] [[rypka1968]] [[browne1906]].

Rumi's son Sultan Walad (d. 1312) and grandson Ulu 'Arif Chalabi organised his followers into the Mevlevi order, whose lodges spread across the Seljuk and then Ottoman lands, with the mother lodge at the poet's tomb in Konya. The Masnavi was read aloud and expounded in these lodges, and commentaries on it were written in Persian, Turkish and Urdu; its ritual of music and turning, the sama', gave the dervishes their Western name of 'whirling dervishes'. The Turkish Republic closed the Sufi lodges in 1925, and the tomb has since been a museum, but the poem has never lost its readers, from the Persian, Ottoman and Indian worlds to the many modern versions in English. This site's text is E. H. Whinfield's translation, which is an abridgement: it renders only a selection of passages in verse and gives the rest in prose summary, and the site prints only the verse. Readers should not take its eighty sections for the whole poem [[whinfield1898]] [[halman1983]] [[lewis2000]].
plot: The Masnavi has no single plot. It opens with the lament of a reed-flute, cut from its reed-bed, that complains of separation and longs to return to its source; this image of the soul exiled from God governs the whole poem. Rumi then tells a story, and within it other stories, each of which raises questions that lead him to further tales or to teaching addressed to the reader. A story may be suspended for hundreds of couplets and taken up again much later, and the 'moral' of one tale often turns into the beginning of the next. This frame-tale method, in which stories open into each other like rooms, is the poem's way of thinking [[safavi2009]] [[nicholson1925]].

Book I begins with the king who falls in love with a handmaid and the divine physician who cures her by uncovering her secret love, and goes on through tales of a parrot, a vizier who destroys a Christian community by deceit, the hare who tricks the lion, the merchant whose parrot escapes its cage by feigning death, the old harper whom the caliph 'Umar honours, and the quarrel of a poor Arab and his wife. Book II, begun after a pause, includes Moses and the shepherd, the man who befriends a bear, and the Sufi whose donkey is starved by a servant. Book III contains the elephant in the dark, the visions of the saint Daquqi, the people of Saba, and the agent who returns to the city that has condemned him because his master's love draws him back.

Book IV contains the lover who escapes the night-watch into a garden and finds his beloved there, Solomon's building of the Farthest Mosque at Jerusalem, Bayazid's ecstatic sayings, and the three fishes of the pond. Book V contains the Prophet's gluttonous unbelieving guest, the peacock who tears out his own feathers, the creation of Adam from earth, and the long story of Sultan Mahmud and his slave Ayaz, who keeps his old shepherd's shoes and sheepskin as a reminder of what he was. Book VI includes the tale of three travellers, a Muslim, a Christian and a Jew, the debtor who comes to Tabriz to find his benefactor dead, and the story of the king's three sons who fall in love with a portrait of a Chinese princess.

That last story breaks off unfinished, and the poem ends there. In a sense this is fitting, for the Masnavi has always insisted that what it points to cannot be put into words. Rumi presents his work as a 'polisher of spirits' and an ocean whose letters and words must in the end fall away. The poem's movement is not towards a conclusion but towards a change in the reader, who is asked to pass from the outward form of the stories to their inner meaning [[schimmel1978]] [[chittick1983]].

books.title: Book I: The Song of the Reed and the Tales of Love
books.lines: About 4,000 couplets in Nicholson's text; Whinfield's Prologue, Stories I–XVI and Epilogue
summary: The poem opens with the Song of the Reed. A reed-flute, torn from its bed, laments its separation; its music moves everyone, but each listener hears only his own feelings in it, and no one understands its secret. The flute's music is 'fire', the fire of love, and the prologue turns to an invocation of Love as the physician of pride, before ending with the image of the heart as a mirror that must be scoured of rust before it can reflect the sun of God.

The first story is that of the king and the handmaid. A king falls in love with a slave girl, who falls ill; his physicians fail, and a holy physician sent by God discovers that she loves a goldsmith of Samarqand. In the middle of this tale Rumi breaks off to speak of Shams of Tabriz and refuses, in a dialogue with his own soul, to say more about him. There follow, among the stories Whinfield keeps, the oilman's parrot who loses its feathers, the Jewish king whose vizier destroys the Christians by deceit, the lion and the beasts (in which a hare outwits the lion and drowns it in a well), 'Umar and the Byzantine envoy, the merchant's parrot who escapes by feigning death, the old harper, the Arab and his wife, the man of Qazvin who wants a lion tattooed on his back but cannot bear the needle, Joseph and the mirror, the contest of the Chinese and Greek painters, and 'Ali's forbearance towards the man who spat in his face. A short epilogue on Adam's fall closes the Book.
analysis: The opening eighteen couplets are the most famous lines in Persian poetry, and they are a key to the whole work. The reed is the soul, its reed-bed is its origin in God, and its music is the speech of a person who has been parted from that source and longs to return. The image also describes the poem itself: the Masnavi is the song of the flute, and it can only be understood by someone who shares its longing. Readers in the Mevlevi tradition took the reed as the emblem of the order, and the flute (ney) became its characteristic instrument [[schimmel1978]] [[lewis2000]].

The story of the king and the handmaid shows Rumi's method at once. On the surface it is a romance of doctors and lovers; but Rumi warns that it is 'the very essence of our state', and the tale becomes an allegory of the soul, the physician of the spirit, and the 'false' love for a creature that must give way to the love of God. The sudden appearance of Shams within the story, and Rumi's refusal to speak of him openly, is the poem's first statement that its real subject can only be approached through veils [[safavi2009]] [[nicholson1925]].

Many of the tales of Book I turn on the difference between appearance and reality, and on the dangers of judging by outward form. The parrots, the deceiving vizier and the painters who polish a wall until it reflects their rivals' pictures all point to the same teaching: the heart must be made empty and clear, like a mirror, so that it can receive what is beyond it. The Joseph story turns this into a doctrine of 'not-being': emptiness and defect are the mirrors in which divine generosity is seen [[chittick1983]].

key.quote:
HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains,
Lamenting its banishment from its home:
key.note: The first couplet of the poem. The Persian begins with the command 'listen' (bishnaw), and Whinfield's archaic 'hearken' keeps its oral character.

key.quote:
The sun (Shams) of Tabriz is a perfect light,
A sun, yea, one of the beams of God!
key.note: Rumi breaks into the story of the king and the handmaid to name Shams, punning on his name, 'sun'.

key.quote:
Since Not-being is the mirror of Being,
If you are wise, choose Not-being (self-abnegation).
key.note: Joseph asks a friend for a gift worthy of him and is given a mirror; the tale becomes a lesson in self-emptying.

key.quote:
The Prophet cried with a loud voice,
'Trust in God, yet tie the camel's leg.'
key.note: The lion's answer to the beasts in the debate on trust in God and the use of means, a theme Rumi returns to throughout the poem.

books.title: Book II: Moses and the Shepherd
books.lines: About 3,800 couplets in Nicholson's text; Whinfield's Prologue and selected Stories
summary: Book II begins with an explanation of the delay: the composition of the Masnavi was interrupted for a season, because 'time is needed for blood to become milk', and resumed when Husam al-Din returned from his spiritual absence, in the year 662 of the Hijra. The Book then opens with the story of the Sufi who leaves his donkey in the care of a servant at a lodge; the servant promises to feed it and does not, and the Sufi is too polite and too credulous to check.

Whinfield's selection goes on to the pauper and the prisoners, the king and his two slaves, the falcon among the owls, the thirsty man who throws bricks into the water to hear its sound, Luqman's master testing his wisdom, Moses and the shepherd, the man who makes a pet of a bear, Bayazid and the saint who tells him that he himself is the Ka'ba, Mu'awiya and Iblis, the old man and the physician, the man who boasts that God does not punish him and the prophet Jethro's answer, the gluttonous Sufi, the tree of life, and the ducklings raised by a hen who return to the water.
analysis: The prologue to Book II, with its image of blood slowly turning into milk, presents poetry as a process of spiritual nourishment that cannot be hurried, and makes Husam al-Din the condition of its making. Rumi calls him 'that light of God', and in every later Book the poet addresses him in the opening lines. The Masnavi thus names its own audience and occasion: it is a teaching given within a relationship of master and disciple [[lewis2000]] [[nicholson1925]].

Moses and the shepherd is the most famous story of the Book. A simple shepherd prays to God in homely terms, offering to comb his hair and wash his clothes, and Moses rebukes him for blasphemy; God then rebukes Moses for driving his servant away. The tale is a statement of the primacy of the heart over correct forms of words, and Rumi expands it into a meditation on the variety of human ways to God. It does not dissolve the law, for Moses remains a prophet; but it shows that sincerity of love can be worth more than theological precision [[chittick1983]] [[schimmel1975]].

The ducklings who leave the hen for the water close Book II with a parable of the soul's true nature: it is born of the sea, though nursed on land. Many of the Book's stories similarly ask how a person can recognise what is real in a world of misleading companions and appearances, and they warn against the 'friends' (the bear, the greedy servant) who promise care and do harm.

key.quote:
THE Composition of this Masnavi has been delayed for a season;
Time is needed for blood to become milk.
key.note: The opening of Book II, on the pause in composition after Book I.

key.quote:
I regard not the outside and the words,
I regard the inside and the state of heart.
key.note: God's reproof to Moses for rebuking the shepherd.

key.quote:
The sect of lovers is distinct from all others,
Lovers have a religion and a faith of their own.
key.note: One of the poem's boldest statements of the religion of love; its context, a divine rebuke to a prophet, keeps it within an Islamic frame.

books.title: Book III: The Elephant in the Dark
books.lines: About 4,800 couplets in Nicholson's text; Whinfield's selected Stories
summary: Whinfield's verse for Book III begins with the travellers who, against a sage's warning, kill and eat a young elephant and are destroyed by its mother, who can smell its flesh on their breath. It continues with the villager who invites a townsman to visit him and treats him with contempt, Moses and Pharaoh, the elephant in a dark room, the lover who reads love poems to his mistress instead of looking at her, the man who prays to be fed without working, the dervish who breaks his vow, the old man who does not mourn his sons, Bahlol and the dervish, and the visions of the saint Daquqi.

There follow the people of Saba, ruined by ingratitude, miracles of the Prophet, the man who asks Moses to teach him the language of animals, the woman who loses all her infants, the agent (vakil) of the prince of Bukhara, who has fled after a fault and returns of his own accord to the city where he is condemned, because love for his master is stronger than fear, and the 'deadly mosque', in which every guest who sleeps there dies, until a brave stranger spends the night in it.
analysis: The parable of the elephant in the dark (which Whinfield gives in prose, keeping in verse Rumi's reflections on it) tells of men who touch an elephant in an unlit room: one feels its trunk and calls it a water-pipe, another an ear and calls it a fan, another a leg and calls it a pillar. Rumi's point is not a comfortable relativism. Each partial perception is mistaken, and the need is for a candle, a vision that sees the whole. The verse that follows contrasts the foam of appearances with the sea that moves it [[nicholson1925]] [[chittick1983]].

Daquqi, a saint who sees seven candles become one and seven trees become one, and then seven men who pray behind him, is the visionary centre of the Book. His story shows Rumi's interest in the hidden company of saints and in the unity behind multiplicity, and it ends with a prayer that saves a sinking ship, an act of compassion that costs the saint his companions' presence [[mojaddedi2012]].

The great passage on the soul's ascent through death, in which the speaker has died as a mineral, a plant and an animal and so need not fear dying as a man, belongs to the story of the agent of Bukhara. It turns the agent's return to death into an image of the lover's willingness to be annihilated, and it is the poem's clearest statement that self-loss is growth [[schimmel1978]].

key.quote:
The sea itself is one thing, the foam another;
Neglect the foam, and regard the sea with your eyes.
key.note: From Rumi's comment on the elephant in the dark: sense perception grasps only the surface of things.

key.quote:
Keep silence, that you may hear Him speaking
Words unutterable by tongue in speech.
key.note: The call to silence (Persian khamush) recurs throughout Rumi's work, in the lyrics as well as the Masnavi.

key.quote:
I died as inanimate matter and arose a plant,
I died as a plant and rose again an animal.
I died as an animal and arose a man.
Why then should I fear to become less by dying?
key.note: The ladder of being, often misread as a theory of evolution; it describes the soul's spiritual ascent through successive deaths.

books.title: Book IV: Lovers, Temples and Fishes
books.lines: About 3,850 couplets in Nicholson's text; Whinfield's selected Stories
summary: Book IV continues a story begun at the end of Book III: a lover pursued by the night-watch climbs over a wall into a garden and finds there the beloved he has long been seeking, so that he blesses the harsh patrol that drove him to her. The Book goes on to Solomon's building of the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa) at Jerusalem, a long section in which the temple becomes an image of the saint's heart, and the youth who writes a letter of complaint to the king about his rations.

Whinfield then gives Bayazid's ecstatic sayings, when the saint, beside himself, declares 'Glory be to me' and his disciples strike at him with knives, only to wound themselves; the three fishes of a pond, the wise, the half-wise and the foolish, who meet the fishermen in different ways; Moses and Pharaoh; the courtier who quarrels with a friend for saving his life; the prince who is bewitched by an old courtesan and then returns to his true love; and the mule and the camel, in which the camel explains why he never stumbles.
analysis: The lover's escape into the garden opens Book IV with a theory of evil: nothing in the world is absolutely bad, since the poison that kills one creature is life to another, and the watchmen's cruelty brought the lover to his joy. The doctrine that evil is relative and serves a higher purpose underlies the poem's treatment of suffering, of Pharaoh and of Iblis [[chittick1983]].

The episode of Bayazid's ecstatic utterance takes up one of the central problems of Sufi history: the 'shath', or ecstatic saying in which a mystic seems to claim divinity. Rumi's explanation is that the annihilated saint has become a mirror, so that whoever strikes at him strikes at his own reflection. The passage defends the ecstatics while making clear that the self has vanished, not that a man has become God [[mojaddedi2012]] [[schimmel1975]].

The three fishes, a fable that Rumi takes from the Kalila wa Dimna tradition, distinguish three kinds of people: the one who has his own light, the one who follows a guide, and the fool who does neither. The scheme is typical of the poem's teaching on the spiritual guide, the shaikh, whom the disciple must follow until he has his own sight [[mojaddedi2012]].

key.quote:
In the world there is nothing absolutely bad;
Know, moreover, evil is only relative.
key.note: The lover's gratitude to the night-watch leads to a doctrine of the relativity of evil.

key.quote:
His form is vanished, he is a mere mirror;
Nothing is seen in him but the reflection of another.
key.note: Rumi's defence of Bayazid's ecstatic sayings: the annihilated saint reflects God.

key.quote:
The wise man is he who possesses a torch of his own;
He is the guide and leader of the caravan.
key.note: The first of the three kinds of people in the fable of the three fishes.

books.title: Book V: Mahmud and Ayaz
books.lines: About 4,250 couplets in Nicholson's text; Whinfield's selected Stories
summary: Book V opens, after its prose preface on the Law, the Path and the Truth, with the story of the unbelieving guest who gorges himself at the Prophet's house and soils his bed in the night, and whom the Prophet washes and forgives; Whinfield's verse begins with the reflections on the outward signs of inward faith that grow from it. There follow the sage who finds a peacock tearing out its beautiful feathers, Sultan Muhammad Khwarazm Shah and the people of Sabzawar, who are ordered to produce a man named Abu Bakr from their Shi'ite town, the man who claimed to be a prophet, the disciple who blindly imitates his shaikh, and the creation of Adam from a handful of earth brought by the angel of death.

The longest story is that of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna and his favourite slave Ayaz, which Whinfield divides in two. Ayaz keeps his old shoes and sheepskin, the clothes of his days as a shepherd, in a locked room and visits them every day; the jealous courtiers suspect hidden treasure, break in, and find nothing else. Between its parts Whinfield gives the repentance of Nasuh, the lion, the fox and the ass, the Muslim who tries to convert a Magian, and the devotee who breaks a nobleman's wine-jar.
analysis: The prose preface to Book V gives the clearest formulation of how Rumi relates religious law to the mystical path: the Law is like a candle that shows the way, the Path is the walking, and the Truth is the arrival. The image matters to the debate about whether Sufism of Rumi's kind dispenses with the law; here the law is the indispensable beginning [[nicholson1925]] [[chittick1983]].

Ayaz is one of the great figures of Persian love-literature, the slave beloved of a king, and Rumi makes him a model of the soul that never forgets its origin. His old shoes and sheepskin remind him of his poverty and protect him from pride; the courtiers, who can only imagine material treasure, represent the carnal soul. The story contains Rumi's sharpest satire of envy and suspicion, and its framing tale of the lover who is 'lost' in his beloved, as vinegar is absorbed in honey, describes annihilation in love [[schimmel1978]].

The peacock who plucks out his feathers because they bring hunters, and the sage who rebukes him, set out the problem of renunciation: whether to flee the world or to live in it with discipline. Rumi favours discipline within society over the hermit's flight, and the debate between them gives Book V its ethical seriousness. In the same Book he asks why one should fear annihilation, since every earlier change of state has been a gain [[chittick1983]].

key.quote:
You have obtained these existences after annihilations;
Wherefore, then, do you shrink from annihilation?
key.note: From the sage's discussion with the peacock: the doctrine of fana as passage to a higher state.

key.quote:
Of my own existence nothing but the name remains
In my being is nothing besides you, O Object of desire!
key.note: The lover's answer in a tale set within the story of Mahmud and Ayaz.

key.quote:
O Ayaz, what is this love of yours for your old shoes,
Which resembles the love of a lover for his mistress?
key.note: The question at the heart of the Ayaz story: why the favourite treasures the signs of his humble past.

books.title: Book VI: The Three Princes and the Unfinished End
books.lines: About 4,900 couplets in Nicholson's text; Whinfield's Prologue and selected Stories
summary: Book VI opens with a dedication to Husam al-Din, the 'life of the heart', and an exhortation to the reader to 'disport' on the island of the Masnavi; it includes a comic anecdote of a student who asks a preacher whether a bird's head or tail is better, which teaches that a person's worth depends on the direction of his aspiration. Whinfield then gives the bird caught by a fowler, the drunken Turkish amir and the minstrel, the purchase of Bilal, the Sufi and the qadi, the poor man who searches for hidden treasure, the three travellers (a Muslim, a Christian and a Jew, who share a sweetmeat and compete with their dreams), and the debtor who travels to Tabriz to seek help from a generous official only to find him dead.

The last story is that of a king's three sons who, warned not to enter a certain fortress, enter it and find there a portrait of a princess of China, with whom they fall in love. They travel to China, where the eldest dies of his longing; the Masnavi breaks off while it is still following the brothers' fortunes, with the third brother's story, in Rumi's phrase, left 'unstrung', and Whinfield's version ends with Rumi's own words on speech breaking down and the rest being told without the tongue.
analysis: The opening of Book VI looks back on the whole poem. Rumi plays on Husam's name, 'sword', and describes the six parts as illuminating the world's six directions, while insisting that love has nothing to do with such dimensions. He imagines a time when the Masnavi will be 'purged of letters and words' and appear as the sea of Unity, a strong statement of the gap between the text and what it points to [[safavi2009]].

The story of the three travellers sets three religious communities side by side, and the Muslim wins not by a superior dream but by eating the sweet while the others sleep, having obeyed a summons from the Prophet. The tale, comic in tone, reflects both Rumi's openness to other faiths and his firm Islamic frame; readers who quote Rumi as a poet beyond religion often overlook such passages [[lewis2000]].

That the Masnavi ends in an unfinished story has prompted much speculation. Later tradition associated the silence with the poet's last illness and death; a 'seventh Book' circulated in the Ottoman period but is not genuine. Whatever its cause, the open ending, with the third prince's story 'unstrung', fits the poem's insistence that its meaning lies beyond words [[lewis2000]] [[nicholson1925]].

key.quote:
O LIFE of the heart, Husamu-'d-Din,
My zeal burnt within me to write this sixth part!
key.note: The opening of the last Book, addressed, like the others, to Husam al-Din.

key.quote:
What is "ascension" to heaven? Annihilation of self;
Self-abandonment is the creed and religion of lovers.
key.note: The ascension (mi'raj) of the Prophet becomes an image of the soul's self-loss.

key.quote:
Here speech, like a camel, breaks down on its road;
I will say no more, but guard my tongue from speech.
key.note: The last lines of Whinfield's version, at the break in the story of the three princes.

characters.name: Jalal al-Din Rumi (the speaker)
characters.text: The poet speaks in his own voice throughout: as storyteller, teacher, commentator and lover. He interrupts his tales to explain them, prays, reproaches his listeners and himself, and often tells himself to be silent. The Masnavi is less a narrative than the record of this voice teaching.

characters.name: Husam al-Din Chalabi
characters.text: Rumi's disciple and successor, at whose request the poem was composed and who wrote it down from dictation. He is addressed at the opening of every Book after the first, called the 'light of God' and the 'life of the heart', and Rumi makes him the condition of the poem's existence. He led Rumi's circle after the poet's death until his own in 1284.

characters.name: Shams al-Din of Tabriz
characters.text: The wandering dervish whose friendship transformed Rumi's life in 1244–1247. In the Masnavi he appears seldom but decisively, as in Book I where Rumi names him and then refuses to reveal his 'secret'. His name, 'Sun of Religion', allows Rumi to merge him with the sun of God.

characters.name: Moses
characters.text: The prophet who appears most often in the poem: rebuked by God for silencing the shepherd, confronting Pharaoh in Books III and IV, and teaching the man who wants to learn the language of animals. He stands for prophetic authority and law, which Rumi respects even when he shows its limits.

characters.name: The shepherd
characters.text: A simple man who prays in homely, anthropomorphic language and is reproved by Moses. God's defence of him makes him the poem's model of sincere, unlearned love.

characters.name: Pharaoh
characters.text: The tyrant who claims to be God, the poem's emblem of the carnal soul and of pride. Rumi gives him moments of hesitation and even sympathy, making him a figure of what resists the divine call within each person.

characters.name: The hare and the lion
characters.text: In the fable of Book I, the beasts agree to send the lion a daily victim; the hare whose turn it is leads the lion to a well, where the lion attacks his own reflection and drowns. The fable becomes a lesson on the 'lion' of the self, whose real enemy is within.

characters.name: The old harper
characters.text: An aged musician, too old to earn his living, who plays for God alone in a graveyard. The caliph 'Umar is sent by a divine voice to provide for him, and the harper repents of his life, but 'Umar teaches him that even his repentance is a kind of self-regard.

characters.name: Bayazid of Bistam
characters.text: The ninth-century Persian Sufi famous for his ecstatic sayings. He appears in Book II, where a saint tells him to circle around him rather than the Ka'ba, and in Book IV, where his disciples attack him for claiming divinity and wound only themselves.

characters.name: Daquqi
characters.text: A wandering saint of Book III who sees visions of seven candles, seven trees and seven men becoming one. His compassionate prayer for a sinking ship ends his companionship with the hidden saints, a paradox about intercession and the divine will.

characters.name: Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna
characters.text: The historical ruler (r. 998–1030), in Persian tradition the type of the powerful king who loves his slave. In Book V he stands for the divine beloved who knows the true worth of his servant.

characters.name: Ayaz
characters.text: Mahmud's favourite, a former shepherd who keeps his old shoes and sheepskin as reminders of his origin. He is the model of humility, loyalty and self-knowledge, and the courtiers' suspicion of him is the poem's study of envy.

characters.name: The agent (vakil) of Bukhara
characters.text: A servant who flees his master after a fault and returns of his own will to the city where he is condemned, because love draws him back. His return to likely death becomes an image of the lover's journey towards annihilation.

characters.name: Noah and Canaan
characters.text: Noah's son, who refuses to enter the ark because he can swim and will climb a mountain, illustrates in Book III the self-reliant intellect that rejects the guide; the flood takes him.

characters.name: Luqman
characters.text: The sage of the Qur'an, in Persian tradition a slave of great wisdom. In Book II his master tests him, and his cleverness shows that wisdom is independent of station.

themes.title: Love
text: Love ('ishq) is the poem's first and last subject. The reed's song is the 'fire of love'; Love is invoked as 'our Plato and our Galen', the physician of pride; and the lover, not the scholar or ascetic, is the poem's ideal. Love in the Masnavi is both a cosmic force that moves all things back towards their source and the particular passion of one person for another, and Rumi uses human love stories, even comic or carnal ones, as ladders towards divine love [[chittick1983]] [[schimmel1978]] [[nicholson1950]].

Rumi is careful to distinguish true love from love of 'forms'. The king's love for the handmaid, the handmaid's love for the goldsmith and the princes' love for a portrait are all stages that must be passed through. But love is never simply condemned: even 'metaphorical' love can become a bridge to the real.

themes.title: Separation and return
text: The Song of the Reed describes a being cut off from its origin, and the longing that this separation produces. The theme draws on the Qur'anic verse 'to Him we shall return' (2:156), which the Masnavi quotes at the climax of the passage on dying from mineral to man. Exile, longing and return form the deep structure of the poem: the ducklings return to the water, the agent returns to Bukhara, and the soul is called back to God [[schimmel1978]].

themes.title: Annihilation (fana) and subsistence
text: The Sufi doctrine of fana, the 'passing away' of the self in God, runs through the poem, together with its complement baqa, 'subsistence' in God after the self has vanished. Rumi speaks of 'not-being' as the workshop of God, of the annihilated saint as a mirror, and of ascension as 'annihilation of self'. Fana is not extinction in a Buddhist sense, nor a claim that the human becomes God; it is the disappearance of the ego, so that only the divine attributes are reflected [[chittick1983]] [[schimmel1975]].

The poem gives this doctrine its most famous image in the ladder of deaths: the soul has died as mineral, plant and animal, and gained at each death; why then should it fear dying to itself? Annihilation becomes the condition of growth.

themes.title: Form and meaning
text: The contrast between form (surat) and meaning (ma'na) is the key to the Masnavi's method. Stories, words and rituals are forms; their value lies in the meaning they carry. The title itself calls the poem a 'masnavi of meaning'. Rumi warns readers not to stop at the husk of the stories, compares words to foam on the sea, and tells God's reproof of Moses, who looked at the shepherd's words instead of his heart [[chittick1983]] [[keshavarz1998]].

Yet Rumi does not despise form: it is the necessary vehicle of meaning, as the body is of the soul. The poem's comic and earthy stories are themselves forms through which the reader must pass, and Rumi's insistence on the law in the preface to Book V shows that outward observance remains the beginning of the way.

themes.title: The guide and the saint
text: Many stories turn on the need for a spiritual guide: the divine physician of Book I, the shaikh whom the disciple must follow, the saint who reflects God. Rumi's teaching on the 'friends of God' (awliya') places the living saint at the centre of religious life, as the one in whom the hidden meaning becomes visible. This teaching connects the Masnavi with the history of Sufi orders and with Rumi's own relationship with Shams and Husam [[mojaddedi2012]].

motifs.title: Stories within stories
motifs.text: Tales are nested inside each other, suspended and resumed, sometimes after many pages. The method imitates the movement of thought and conversation, and it forces the reader to look for connections of meaning rather than of plot.

motifs.title: Qur'an and hadith
motifs.text: The poem quotes and paraphrases the Qur'an and the sayings of the Prophet on almost every page. Whinfield marks many of these quotations with inverted commas; they are the hidden scaffolding of Rumi's arguments.

motifs.title: Animal fables
motifs.text: Lions, hares, foxes, parrots, peacocks, camels and fish carry much of the teaching, as they do in the Kalila wa Dimna tradition. Rumi uses them both for practical wisdom and for allegories of the soul.

motifs.title: Silence
motifs.text: The narrator repeatedly tells himself to stop speaking, and the poem ends in silence. Rumi's lyrics often close with the word khamush, 'silent', and the Masnavi shares this sense that the highest truths cannot be spoken.

symbols.title: The reed-flute
symbols.text: The soul cut off from its origin and singing of its longing; also the poet, the poem, and the perfected human being, empty of self so that God's breath can sound through him. The ney became the emblem of the Mevlevi order.

symbols.title: The mirror
symbols.text: The heart, which must be polished of rust to reflect God; the annihilated saint, who reflects whoever looks at him; and 'not-being', in which Being shows itself. The Chinese and Greek painters of Book I make the image into a parable.

symbols.title: The sun
symbols.text: God, the source of all light, and Shams of Tabriz, whose name means 'sun'. Rumi exploits the pun to merge his friend with the divine light he revealed.

symbols.title: Sea and foam
symbols.text: The ocean of divine reality and the surface of appearances. The image recurs from Book III's comment on the elephant to Book VI's vision of the Masnavi as the 'sea of Unity'.

symbols.title: Wine and cup
symbols.text: The meaning and the form; the divine gift and the vessel that holds it. Rumi warns against being intoxicated with 'goblets of forms' instead of the wine they contain.

debates.title: Is the Masnavi designed or spontaneous?
text: The poem was dictated over many years, and its digressions and suspended stories have often been taken as a sign that it is spontaneous and associative, the record of a teacher speaking to his circle. Many readers have treated it as a collection of tales and teachings to be read in excerpts, as Whinfield's and Arberry's selections encourage [[whinfield1898]] [[arberry1961]].

Seyed Ghahreman Safavi and Simon Weightman argued, on the contrary, that Book I has a deliberate design: its stories are arranged in parallel and ring patterns around a centre, so that the order of the tales is itself part of the meaning. Their reading has prompted debate about whether every Book is structured in this way and how far such patterns would have been perceived by Rumi's audience [[safavi2009]].

debates.title: Rumi and Ibn 'Arabi
text: Rumi's contemporary in Konya, Sadr al-Din Qunawi, was the chief disciple of the great Andalusian mystic Ibn 'Arabi, and later commentators, especially in the Ottoman world, read the Masnavi through Ibn 'Arabi's metaphysics of the 'oneness of being' (wahdat al-wujud). William Chittick argued that this reading distorts Rumi, whose teaching is practical and centred on love rather than on systematic metaphysics, though the two share many ideas. The relationship between the two traditions remains a central question in the study of Persian Sufism [[chittick1983]] [[lewis2000]].

debates.title: Who was Shams, and what happened to him?
text: Most of what was said about Shams for centuries came from hagiographies written after Rumi's death, especially Aflaki's Manaqib al-'arifin, which tells of his murder. Modern scholars treat these sources critically. Lewis points out that the murder story appears late and is unproven, and Chittick's translation of Shams's own Maqalat reveals a figure quite different from the legend: a learned, sharp-tongued teacher with firm views on the Prophet and the law [[lewis2000]] [[chittick2004]] [[okane2002]].

debates.title: Islam and the Western Rumi
text: In the late twentieth century Rumi became one of the best-selling poets in the United States, largely through free versions such as Coleman Barks's, which present him as a poet of universal spirituality. Scholars have pointed out that such versions often detach the poems from the Qur'anic and Islamic context that saturates the Masnavi, and that they rarely draw on the Masnavi's narratives at all [[barks1995]] [[lewis2000]].

The question is not only one of accuracy. Rumi's openness to other faiths, visible in stories like that of the three travellers, is real, but it is expressed within an Islamic understanding of revelation. Readers must hold together the poem's universality and its specific religious frame [[lewis2000]] [[schimmel1975]].

debates.title: Sainthood and authority
text: Jawid Mojaddedi reads the Masnavi against earlier Sufi theories of sainthood (walaya) and argues that the 'friend of God', the living saint, is the centre of its teaching, more important than formal learning or doctrine. On this reading the poem's frequent criticism of scholars and literalists is not anti-intellectual, but a claim about where religious authority lies; it also helps explain the poem's role in founding an order [[mojaddedi2012]].

debates.title: Law and ecstasy
text: Stories like Moses and the shepherd, and Rumi's defence of Bayazid's ecstatic sayings, have led some readers to see Rumi as indifferent to religious law. The preface to Book V, which presents the Law as the candle that lights the Path, and Rumi's own life as a jurist and preacher, point the other way. Most scholars now see him as holding the two together: law as the necessary form, love as its meaning [[chittick1983]] [[schimmel1978]].

debates.title: Translating and abridging the Masnavi
text: English readers first met the Masnavi through the Victorian versions of James Redhouse, who translated Book I, and E. H. Whinfield, who abridged all six Books into a selection of passages. Nicholson's complete literal translation with commentary (1925–1940) remains the scholarly standard, and Mojaddedi's verse translation for Oxford World's Classics has made the complete text readable again. Abridgements shape what readers think the poem is: by keeping the tales and cutting much of the teaching, they make the Masnavi look like a book of fables [[redhouse1881]] [[whinfield1898]] [[nicholson1925]] [[mojaddedi2004]].

quotes.quote:
HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains,
Lamenting its banishment from its home:
quotes.explanation: The poem's opening: the reed's lament for its lost reed-bed is the soul's longing for God, and the image governs the whole work.

quotes.quote:
This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air.
Let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead!
quotes.explanation: The flute's breath is the fire of love; without it a person is spiritually dead. The lines set the poem's measure of life.

quotes.quote:
If it were purified from all rust and defilement,
It would reflect the shining of the SUN Of GOD.
quotes.explanation: The heart as a mirror, one of the poem's master images; the spiritual path is the polishing of the mirror.

quotes.quote: Naught but Love itself can explain love and lovers!
quotes.explanation: The limits of reason and language before love, a recurrent theme of the poem.

quotes.quote:
Kindle in thy heart the flame of love,
And burn up utterly thoughts and fine expressions.
quotes.explanation: God's defence of the shepherd's simple prayer: the heart outweighs correct words.

quotes.quote:
The eye of outward sense is as the palm of a hand,
The whole of the object is not grasped in the palm.
quotes.explanation: The moral of the elephant in the dark: the senses grasp only part of reality.

quotes.quote:
I died as inanimate matter and arose a plant,
I died as a plant and rose again an animal.
quotes.explanation: The ladder of being, in which every death has been a gain; the passage argues that the soul need not fear dying to itself.

quotes.quote:
To the creatures of the sea the sea is a garden,
To the creatures of the land it is fatal.
quotes.explanation: The relativity of good and evil, illustrated from nature.

quotes.quote:
So, when the Masnavi is purged of letters and words,
It drops all these, and appears as the sea of Unity.
quotes.explanation: The poem's account of itself: its words are a surface that must fall away to reveal what lies beneath.

quotes.quote:
Form proceeds from the world that is without form,
Even as smoke arises from fire.
quotes.explanation: The relation of form and meaning in a single image: visible forms come from an invisible source.

questions.q: How does the Song of the Reed prepare the reader for the rest of the Masnavi?
questions.hint: Consider separation and return, the listener who hears only his own feelings, the fire of love and the mirror at the end of the prologue.

questions.q: Why does Rumi tell stories within stories instead of setting out his teaching directly?
questions.hint: Think about form and meaning, the reader's active role, and the suspended stories of Book I.

questions.q: What is the role of Husam al-Din in the poem, and why does Rumi address him at the start of the Books?
questions.hint: Look at the prologues to Books II and VI and the poem's origin in a master–disciple relationship.

questions.q: How does Rumi treat Shams of Tabriz in the Masnavi compared with the lyric poetry of the Divan?
questions.hint: Look at the interruption in the story of the king and the handmaid and the pun on 'sun'.

questions.q: What does the story of Moses and the shepherd teach about the relationship between religious law and love?
questions.hint: Consider God's reproof of Moses, and then the preface to Book V on Law, Path and Truth.

questions.q: Explain the doctrine of fana as the Masnavi presents it. Is it a doctrine of extinction?
questions.hint: Use the passage on dying from mineral to man, the saint as mirror, and 'ascension' as annihilation of self.

questions.q: What does the parable of the elephant in the dark say about knowledge, and what does it not say?
questions.hint: Distinguish partial perception from relativism; note the candle and the sea and foam.

questions.q: How do animal fables function in the Masnavi? Choose two examples.
questions.hint: The lion and the hare, the three fishes, the peacock, the mule and the camel.

questions.q: What does the story of Ayaz's old shoes and sheepskin reveal about humility and envy?
questions.hint: Consider what the courtiers expect to find and what Ayaz keeps.

questions.q: How does reading Whinfield's abridgement shape our impression of the poem? What is lost?
questions.hint: Compare the number of sections here with the length of the full poem, and consider what an abridger keeps.
